prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms held at a magic wavelength enable timekeeping and frequency measurement at the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a concrete invention that fits the discovery-or-invention criterion: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the trap-induced shift while keeping many atoms interrogated, and Ye's group carried it to the 1e-18 regime with many-body control. Four colleagues placed it first and I ranked it second, so this is the one candidate with broad support across subfields rather than one member's enthusiasm. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: two names that match the proposal-plus-realisation split, with no collaboration-size problem and no need to drop a credited person. It has been reproduced independently at the 1e-18 level and compared internationally for about two decades. As an experimentalist I value that the claim is a measurement that others can repeat and compare.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is distinctness. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and the 2012 prize covered control of single trapped ions, which underlie optical clocks, so some will see lattice clocks as the next increment in an already honoured line. The redefinition of the second has not happened, so the largest practical consequence is still pending, and credit for Sr and Yb clock development at PTB, NIST, SYRTE and elsewhere falls outside the two credited names. Choosing it also means setting aside my own first-ranked candidate, magic-angle graphene, for reasons of maturity and credit rather than because the physics is less interesting.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked lattice clocks first as a clean, mature two-person configuration, but placed twisted bilayer graphene third and flagged that its pairing mechanism is unresolved, that recognition may be early, and that the experimental credit is spread over several groups and includes a junior first author outside the credited names.
responses.response: I agree with the clock case and I concede most of the graphene reservations. I ranked B010 first because it is a materials discovery resting on well characterised structures, but the experimental credit problem is real: the 2018 observation depended on a junior first author who cannot be credited, and my proposed pair leaves out Bistritzer. The disputed pairing mechanism is a limit on the interpretation, not on the discovery, but it makes the claim less settled than the clock result. I would keep B010 as an alternative for a later year, not as this year's preferred prize.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance second, arguing that the Moodera and Miyazaki 1995 observations are the decisive discovery, that it is long confirmed and arguably overdue, and that the main complication is whether the MgO coherent-tunnelling step and Parkin must be included.
responses.response: I ranked B009 fourth and still think it is a serious candidate. My reservation is about scope, not merit. The 1995 observation and the MgO symmetry-filtering step are different achievements, and the second was later and involved Parkin, Yuasa and the theorists Butler and Mathon. A prize honouring only the first would understate where the large effect and the devices came from, and a prize honouring both gets past three people. Unless the committee can agree on which step is the discovery, I think B009 is less secure than the clocks, and I would keep it as a second alternative. I am open to being convinced if you think the 1995 step stands alone, given the overlap with the 2007 GMR prize.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked lattice clocks first and called the two-person configuration natural, but placed twisted bilayer graphene third and said that with the field under a decade old and the superconducting mechanism disputed, recognition could be premature.
responses.response: I now think your maturity argument against B010 is stronger than I gave it credit for in my opening. A field less than a decade old with an unresolved pairing mechanism is a harder case than one with two decades of cross-laboratory comparison. Where I qualify your view is that the maturity test should be about whether the discovery is robust, and flat-band correlated states have been reproduced widely. That is why I keep it as an alternative. On the clocks, I would press you and Pearce on the prior-recognition point: you cite the 2005 prize as supporting timing, but it can equally be read as showing that this line has already been honoured.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED first, arguing that it is the architecture behind modern superconducting processors, with a genuine allocation problem between Blais and Girvin, and noted that he works in this subfield.
responses.response: I do not dispute the importance of circuit QED. My concern is the same one you raise: the 2025 prize was in adjacent superconducting-circuit physics, and a four-name credit list forces an omission between Blais and Girvin. I would be reluctant to give two prizes in this neighbourhood in consecutive years while a clean two-name candidate is available. I also note that you ranked lattice clocks eighth, so I would like to hear whether that is a judgement about the physics or about prior recognition of metrology.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 trapped-ion prizes.
Whether credit for the lattice-clock concept and the first Sr demonstrations is fully captured by Katori and Ye, since other strontium and ytterbium groups are outside the supplied names.
Whether the unresolved pairing mechanism and the credit spread make magic-angle graphene premature this year or only a matter of waiting a few more years.
I have not verified the detailed history of the early experimental credit for twisted bilayer graphene or for MgO tunnel junctions.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B004, B010 or B009. I have no documented tie to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Moodera, Miyazaki or Parkin. My general microscopy and Japanese academic connections and my Chalmers affiliation, shared with Göran Johansson, whose first-ranked candidate is B034, are noted for transparency but do not bear on my preferred configuration.
